title: Berthoud Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Berthoud wells have a 27-foot median depth, but deeper wells occur. See yields, water levels, permit history, risks and drilling costs.
h1: Berthoud, Colorado Well Depths, Yields and Costs
intro_html:
Well records within five miles of Berthoud show a plains setting where many wells are shallow, but the local range is wide. The median reported depth is 27 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 1,000 feet. That spread matters when you are pricing a property: a nearby well is useful evidence, but it does not guarantee the same depth or water production on your lot.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records for Berthoud and nearby Weld County areas. The records include domestic, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells, so they are not all direct comparisons for a household well.

sections.heading: Berthoud’s shallow median hides a wide drilling range
sections.html:
Berthoud wells have a 27-foot median reported depth, and the middle half runs from 16 to 44 feet. That is an unusually shallow central range for estimating a basic borehole in this plains setting. Still, 87% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while the local record also includes wells from 100 to 300 feet, 300 to 600 feet, and above 600 feet.

For a driller’s bid, do not price every parcel from the median alone. The 90th-percentile depth is 240 feet, and the deepest record is 1,000 feet. Local alluvium, plains sedimentary rock, the intended use, and the exact water-bearing layer can change the job substantially. Nearby records from Johnstown, Mead, Milliken, Platteville, Firestone and Gilcrest can help establish context, but a site-specific estimate still requires a driller’s review.

sections.heading: What Berthoud wells produce for a household
sections.html:
Among the Berthoud-area records that report pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 5.0 to 104.0 gallons per minute, showing a broad spread between modest household wells and much stronger-producing wells. The yield data are limited: only 34 permits report a pump yield, so treat the statistic as a guide rather than a promise for an untested parcel.

Six percent of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, and 9% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. That low-producing minority deserves attention during a purchase. A household may function on a low-yield well with adequate storage, but irrigation, livestock, multiple bathrooms or future construction can increase demand. Have the well tested for production and recovery, not just water quality.

sections.heading: The water table is shallow, but the records do not show a trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a 12-foot median depth to water, with the middle half between 7 and 16 feet. In practical terms, many recorded wells encounter relatively shallow groundwater. That can reduce drilling depth, but it also means groundwater may be more exposed to surface conditions, poor well construction or nearby contamination sources.

The available facts provide a water-level summary, not a decade-by-decade series. They do not support a conclusion that the water table is rising or dropping over time. Static level is also not the same as a sustained pumping level. Ask for the original well construction report, static and pumping measurements, and any recent service records. A shallow water level does not by itself establish a reliable household supply or safe drinking water.

sections.heading: Recent permits and the contractors in the record
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show 682 permitted wells within five miles of Berthoud, with 315 recorded as constructed. A newer permit may describe an intended well rather than a completed and tested water source, so separate construction records from permit records when researching a property. The newest permit year in this dataset is 2026, and 75 permits were issued in the 2020s.

The most active driller name in these records is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 278 records. Kelley Dewatering And Construction Company (Creech, Jason) appears on 34, and Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed) appears on 17. These entries reflect permit records and do not mean every listed contractor is available for new work. Confirm current licensing, scope and insurance before hiring.

sections.heading: A Berthoud well budget starts with depth, not just footage
sections.html:
For Berthoud’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $900 to $1,500. That is only the drilling portion. It does not represent a complete operating water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $6,900 to $13,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, hard formation, storage needs and long utility runs can move the total outside that range. Before buying land, request an itemized bid that separates drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical and testing. Confirm what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: Berthoud risks: water quality, low yield and site layout
sections.html:
The mapped area within about ten miles includes 1,198 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, five historic mine features and five EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site is a reason to investigate, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. Order a qualified drinking-water test for the property and ask about nearby land uses, historic activities and any recorded sampling.

Low yield and dry-hole risk also need a written plan. Six percent of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, and the dataset includes only 34 yield reports. Check the well construction, casing and grout, pump test results, storage capacity and service history. Septic location, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, utility trenches and the proposed building footprint must be planned together. A shallow well and a shallow groundwater level can make septic separation and construction decisions especially important.

sections.heading: What to check before buying or building near Berthoud
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and construction records for the property, then compare several nearby wells rather than relying on one neighbor. Look at depth, aquifer description, static water level, reported yield and intended use. Berthoud records name 317 wells in an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 159 in alluvial aquifers and nine in Quaternary Alluvium; 18% are identified with Denver Basin aquifers. Those labels show local variety, not a guaranteed result for your lot.

For a purchase, make the contract contingent on reviewing the permit, testing water quality and confirming the well serves the intended use. For a build, obtain a driller’s access and depth estimate before finalizing the house site. Household use, irrigation, stock water and monitoring permits are not interchangeable. Also confirm whether an augmentation plan is needed in an over-appropriated basin and verify the permit’s allowed uses with Colorado DWR.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Berthoud, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Berthoud is 27 feet, with the middle half between 16 and 44 feet. Most reported wells, 87%, are under 100 feet. Depth still varies substantially: the 90th-percentile depth is 240 feet and the deepest recorded well is 1,000 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Berthoud?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At Berthoud’s 27-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $900 to $1,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $6,900 to $13,500. Deeper drilling, access and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Berthoud well produce?
faq.a: Among the 34 Berthoud-area records reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with a middle-half range of 5.0 to 104.0 gallons per minute. Six percent report under 1 gallon per minute. Because yield records are limited, order a production or recovery test before relying on a well for a home or irrigation.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Berthoud?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a well is safe to drink. The mapped area includes 1,198 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about ten miles, along with five historic mine features and five EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory and review construction, septic conditions and nearby land uses.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well near Berthoud?
faq.a: Building may be possible, but the permit must allow the intended household use and the well must provide an adequate supply. Review the DWR permit, construction report, yield and water quality. Plan the well, septic system, building footprint, access and utility trenches together. Confirm any augmentation-plan requirement and other water-right conditions before closing or starting construction.
